Investment memo · 17 November 2026

Alcon (ALC-CH): a dependable 10% earnings compounder on a floor multiple, whose re-rating needs both the premium-lens worry and the medtech sector's de-rating to clear

17 November 2026. Share price CHF 61.36 on the Swiss line ($73.21 in New York) at the 13 November close. Figures are in US dollars on the company's core (adjusted) basis unless stated; "cc" means constant currency and "bp" means basis points. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model after update 1, with no input changed (topic #6 explains why). Source notes are at the end.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

Alcon's earnings are dependable, its re-rating is not, and the shares are priced as if the earnings were the uncertain part. Alcon is the world's largest eye-care company. About 70% of its sales (surgical consumables, contact lenses and eye drops) is an annuity that grows 5% to 8% a year with little forecasting error. That annuity, a cost line that management steers to an earnings target, and a share buyback together compound core EPS at about 10% to 11% a year to 2030. The shares nonetheless trade on 17.2 times two-year-forward earnings, the 1st percentile of their history since the 2019 listing. The market is judging the whole company on one product line: premium cataract lenses in the United States, where Johnson & Johnson's PureSee lens has taken share and Alcon's implant sales fell in the third quarter of 2026. A re-rating therefore needs two things. The premium-lens worry must clear, which Alcon's own reported figures cannot show before August 2027, and the de-rated medtech sector must recover.

Where the skew liesThe positive skew Richard looks for is present in the multiple and absent in the estimates. This is a case about valuation and time, not about upgrades.

The eight things that matter most

  1. Alcon's earnings and its share price have different drivers. FY2027 EPS is predictable to within about 5%, but the multiple is set by the sector and by a product line estimated at only 4% to 5% of group sales. Three EPS beats in 2026 did not lift the shares.
  2. This is not an upgrade story. Guidance is realistic, not conservative, and our forecasts sit about 1% below the brokers who have updated since the third-quarter results. Estimate revisions will look negative into mid-2027. The case therefore fails Richard's test of positively skewed outcomes and upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months; it passes on valuation and on time.
  3. The news arrives in an unhelpful order. Alcon's three reports most likely to disappoint (2 March, May and August 2027) come before the three with easy comparisons (November 2027 to May 2028).
  4. Time works for the holder. With no change in the multiple, earnings growth and dividends alone return about 17% by March 2028 and about 33% by September 2029. A fall to the 14.5x trough multiple, with estimates 5% lower, costs about 6% by March 2028 and roughly breaks even over three years.
  5. The model's +52.9% return to March 2028 leans on a re-rating that the forecasts do not earn on their own. 30.8 points of that return come from the multiple rising to the 22.51x guideline, while four separate routes put the multiple Alcon can earn by itself at about 19.5x to 20x. My probability-weighted return is +20% to +25%.
  6. Two positives are barely discussed. First, a higher tax rate hid 2 to 2.5 points of operating EPS growth in 2026, so Alcon's durable growth rate is better evidenced than the "2026 was flattered" narrative allows. Second, net debt is heading to about 0.7x EBITDA by end-2028, which will force management to choose between more buybacks and acquisitions.
  7. Three near-dated negatives are also barely discussed. China's procurement price cuts hit reported implant sales from January 2027, which will blur the reading on Alcon's new Vivity Pro lens. A quarter of 2027 revenue growth rests on two drug launches (Tryptyr and ENCELTO) that need skills Alcon has not yet shown. And a third competitor lens, from Bausch + Lomb, arrives in 2027.
  8. The stock is bottoming, not yet turning up. The dashboard rates valuation A, sell-side earnings momentum F and technical momentum D.

Dates to hold in mind. January 2027: Vivity Pro launches in the United States. Mid-January and mid-April 2027: Johnson & Johnson reports results, giving the earliest hard read on the premium-lens contest. 2 March 2027: Alcon reports FY2026 results and gives formal 2027 guidance. August 2027: Alcon's second-quarter report, the first that can show a clean implant recovery.

#1Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

Alcon's markets grow steadily but slowly, at about 4% to 5% a year, so its own growth has to come from product mix, new products and margin. Cataract procedures grow about 3% a year globally, against 4% to 5% historically, and were flat in the United States in 2026. The constraint is surgeon capacity, not patient demand, and management assumes about 3% procedure growth again for 2027. Contact lens markets grow 4% to 5% in value: 5% to 6% in the United States and 1% to 2% elsewhere, where online sellers and private-label lenses hold prices down. Prescription dry-eye treatment grows at double digits.

The strongest tailwind, the shift to premium cataract lenses, paid mostly Alcon's rivals in 2026. Patients pay for premium lenses themselves. Medicare cut the surgeon's fee for cataract surgery by 11% in 2026 and will cut it by a further 3% to 4% in 2027, so surgeons promote premium lenses to protect their income. As a result, United States premium penetration rose about 200bp in the first half of 2026, against 50 to 100bp a year previously.

Alcon's 2026 tailwinds were one-offs, and its list of headwinds is longer for 2027. The tariff refund and the weaker dollar will not repeat, while tariffs without a refund, China's procurement cuts and a de-rated medtech sector all weigh on 2027.

Tailwinds

  • Premium-lens shift: US penetration up about 200bp in H1 2026, against 50 to 100bp a year before
  • Medicare fee cuts: -11% in 2026, a further -3% to -4% for 2027, so surgeons promote premium lenses
  • Prescription dry eye: double-digit growth
  • 2026 one-offs, gone in 2027: $58m tariff refund; a weaker dollar

Headwinds, longer for 2027

  • Tariffs: $80m to $100m a year gross, with no refund
  • China procurement: second round cuts lens prices 30% to 50% from January 2027 on $125m to $143m of sales
  • Inputs: memory chips and resins add about 20bp of cost
  • Slow procedures: cataract about 3% globally (4% to 5% historically), flat in the US in 2026
  • Sector: medtech median 17.1x, 2nd percentile of its history; US ten-year yield near 5%

Inference and so-what. The environment supports a 5% grower, not an accelerating one. Because Alcon's markets grow 4% to 5%, its faster growth must come from mix and new products, and its margin gains from inside the company. The environment is mildly worse in 2027 than it was in 2026, and the headwinds are real.

Strongest counter-case. The Medicare fee cuts are structural, and Alcon still holds the largest share of premium lenses. If Alcon's premium share merely stops falling, a premium segment growing at high single digits turns straight into 3% to 5% implant growth. Surgeon capacity could also ease, which would lift volumes for Alcon as the owner of more than 80% of United States cataract consoles. Against that, patients pay about 60% of Alcon's revenue out of pocket, so a consumer downturn would hit premium lenses first.

What would change my view. More positive: United States procedure growth above 2%, tariff relief, or third-party data showing Alcon's premium-lens share steady for two quarters. More negative: Section 301 tariffs enacted on Swiss and European imports, or Chinese price cuts at the top of the 30% to 50% range.

Against the market. I agree with the consensus view of about 3% procedure growth, but I differ on two points. First, the market reads the Medicare fee cuts as a negative for Alcon. The cuts are a mix tailwind for whichever company holds premium share, and the 2027 Medicare rules also raise the facility payment to ambulatory surgery centres by 2.3%, which eases the worry about those centres' capital budgets. Second, no one has yet connected the January 2027 start of China's price cuts to Alcon's first-half 2027 implant figures, which the cuts will drag by about 2 points regardless of how the new lens performs.

Conclusion: the external environment is a steady 4% to 5% base with one strong tailwind, premium lenses, that is currently paying Alcon's rivals, and the environment is mildly worse in 2027 than in 2026.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. Demand is steady but slow (cataract procedures about 3%, flat in the US in 2026; contact lenses 4-5%), and the structural premium-lens shift pushed by Medicare fee cuts is currently paying J&J's PureSee, while 2027 adds external headwinds ($80-100m gross tariffs with no refund, China procurement cuts of 30-50% on $125-143m of sales, input costs) after one-off 2026 tailwinds. That is a slightly net negative environment, below Kerry's neutral one and above Carlsberg's mature one, coherent with the group's 46.

#2Internally driven corporate change

Alcon's internal changes are broad and well funded, but the negative changes sit in premium optics, exactly where the multiple is set. The positives are a full launch slate, a larger savings programme and a new buyback. The negatives are a failed in-house premium lens, restructuring that costs more than planned, and mid-term targets that management has let slip.

Inference and so-what. These changes sustain Alcon's trajectory rather than raise it: they support 10% to 11% EPS growth without heroics. The one internal event that could move the share price is the United States launch of Vivity Pro in January 2027.

The missing change is a decision by management to put margin first. There is room for 200 to 300bp of margin improvement over three to four years, mostly in selling and administrative costs, but management says it values growth over margin. A new cost programme of $150 to $200 million aimed at margin, rather than at offsetting inflation, would add 130 to 170bp by 2029 to 2030 and is the cleanest route to estimate upgrades. The only visible source of pressure is Pershing Square, which bought shares during the 2026 de-rating and argues for margins above 25%; it has reported no engagement with the board.

Strongest counter-case. I may be under-rating the launches. Unity renews a ten-year consumables stream and is already installed in 40% of United States teaching hospitals. New contact lens capacity is coming on stream. The corneal cell therapy AURN001, with approval targeted for late 2028, has peak sales above $500 million on one broker's estimate. Together, these launches could lift revenue growth above 5% from 2028.

What would change my view. More positive: a margin-first programme or a larger buyback announced on 2 March 2027, or a formal reset of the mid-term targets with a credible bridge (Coloplast's shares rose 4% on such a reset this month). More negative: a second problem beside implants, such as another large impairment or receivables and inventories outrunning sales, or a large acquisition.

Against the market. The market is watching Vivity Pro. I think management's spending choices move 2027 EPS more than the new lens does (topic #5), and almost no one has sized those choices.

Conclusion: internal change is broad, funded and sufficient to sustain about 10% EPS growth, but nothing under way raises the trajectory, and the lever that would raise it, a margin-first stance, has not been pulled.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. Broad, funded positives (the fullest launch slate in its history including new drug lines Tryptyr and ENCELTO, $130m of savings, a $1.5bn buyback) are offset by the PowerVision write-off, three years of trimmed guidance, 2027 targets to be missed by about $0.4bn and 300bp, restructuring costs up from $150m to $230m and no change in leadership or ambition. In Richard's CVS terms this is gently positive but mediocre change that sustains rather than raises the trajectory, a little above Shell and the group's 53 because the new product lines are a real extension.

#3Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Alcon leads tight oligopolies, and three-quarters of its business compounds mechanically; the exception is premium cataract lenses, where share swings with each new optic. Alcon is the largest company in a $35 billion eye-care market, and its markets are protected by regulatory, clinical and manufacturing barriers.

29%of a $35bn eye-care market
45%cataract lenses, number one
about halfsurgical consoles and consumables, number one
about 26%contact lenses, number two, a record share
85% to 90%held by the top four (about 85% of cataract lenses, about 90% of contact lenses)

Evidence: the business model. Most of the business compounds mechanically. A console locks a clinic into Alcon's single-use surgical packs for seven to ten years, and about 40% of consumables are tied to Alcon hardware. Contact lens wearers repurchase the same brand about 80% of the time.

Premium cataract lenses behave differently, because surgeons choose them case by case and switching costs are low. Alcon's United States premium share rose from 35% in 2019 to over 80% in 2021 and has fallen back toward 60% now, as each maker launched a better optic. Alcon's rebates slow switching: clinics that keep about 90% of their lens volume with Alcon earn about 30% back. Once a rival's free samples push a clinic below that threshold, however, the clinic loses the rebate, its remaining Alcon lenses cost more, and its reason to stay weakens. Alcon's rebate is therefore a moat until it is breached and an accelerator of share loss afterwards. That mechanism explains why Alcon's share fell in steps, and why I expect the share to stabilise rather than rebound.

Evidence: financial profile. Alcon's financial profile is above average, with one blemish in earnings quality. Reported return on capital is only 5% to 6%, mainly because of goodwill inherited at the 2019 spin-off but also because about $3 billion of acquisitions since 2022 has yet to earn a return. Core earnings also exclude a great deal: FY2025 core EPS was $3.07 against $1.99 reported. Acquired research never passes through the core accounts, so Alcon's true innovation spending is 13% to 15% of sales, not the 8% to 9% that the core accounts show.

Above average

  • Core operating margin about 21%, level with Sonova and Smith & Nephew and far above Carl Zeiss Meditec
  • Net debt 1.4x EBITDA, 98% at fixed rates
  • Cash generation 90% to 100% of core net income

The blemish: earnings quality

Evidence: management. Alcon's management is capable, stable and well resourced, but not exceptional. It has built the business well (core margin up 340bp from 2019 to 2024) and has walked away from two large acquisitions on price. It has also been out-executed by Johnson & Johnson in premium lenses twice in two years, and it has let its mid-term targets slip without resetting them.

Inference and so-what. Three-quarters of the business sits where industry structure and scale work in Alcon's favour, and that advantage widens with time. The remaining quarter, the most profitable, sits where structure and scale do not protect Alcon. That split explains why Alcon's earnings are safe and its share price is not.

Strongest counter-case. Customer consolidation is eroding the product bundle that protects Alcon's surgical share. Private-equity-owned surgery centres now perform about 20% of United States cataract procedures and buy from several vendors. If bundling weakens, Alcon's premium-lens problem stops being a product cycle and becomes structural.

What would change my view. Consumables growth below procedure growth for several quarters, which would show the bundle failing, or a break in contact lens price discipline in the United States.

Against the market. Bulls assert that Alcon's installed base of consoles protects its premium lenses. The evidence says the installed base protects consumables and only slows lens switching. Bears treat the premium-lens problem as a verdict on the whole franchise. I think both overreach: Alcon is a strong franchise with one exposed edge.

Conclusion: Alcon's industry structure and three-quarters of its business model are top-tier and self-reinforcing, its financial profile is above average with an earnings-quality blemish, and its management is good but not exceptional.

Score: 71, set by the Rater. Structure and moat are near top-tier (number one in cataract lenses at 45%, consoles and consumables, number two in contact lenses, oligopolies where the top four hold 85-90%, 7-10 year console lock-in and about 80% brand repurchase, a predictable 70% annuity), but the premium-lens moat has narrowed (US share from over 80% to about 60%), reported ROIC is 3.6% (27th percentile; goodwill-distorted, yet about $3bn of post-2022 deals is not earning), core EPS far exceeds reported, and management is good not exceptional. Above Tele2's sound oligopoly, short of Tenaris on returns on new capital, coherent with the groups (74, 70, 55, 57).

#4Guidance: conservatism, and the record of delivery and raises

Alcon's guidance is realistic rather than conservative: management reliably lands the EPS number, misses on revenue, and has not raised guidance on operating performance. For FY2026 the company guides sales growth of about 6% cc, core operating margin expansion of 100 to 150bp, and core EPS growth of 12% to 14% cc, which is about $3.49 to $3.55. For 2027 it has given an early frame: underlying operating leverage of 150 to 200bp, net margin expansion of under 100bp, and growth at the low end of its 6% to 8% target range.

The guidance record has three features.

  • The 2026 guidance raises were not operating raises. May's raise came from the lower share count (the new buyback) and August's from the tariff refund. The operating guide was met at its original midpoint and then trimmed in November.
  • Sales or margin guidance has been lowered or trimmed during each of 2024, 2025 and 2026, including two outright cuts in 2025.
  • Revenue has missed consensus in seven of the last nine quarters, while EPS has beaten in seven, because management flexes costs to land the earnings number.

Inference. Alcon's guidance therefore contains no hidden cushion. What management does well is manage expectations. By giving the 2027 frame four months early, it walked the brokers to where the formal guide will land, so that the guide is met on the day it is published. One broker explicitly welcomed that tone.

My probabilities follow from that record. The most likely outcome on 2 March is a formal 2027 EPS guide within 1% of the updated brokers' $3.84. During 2027 a cut to EPS guidance is slightly likelier than a raise, and the sales range has about an even chance of being lowered or narrowed to its lower half. The 2028 guide, due around March 2028, has a 60% or better chance of a midpoint below today's FactSet median of $4.40.

So-what. A case built on guidance upgrades is not on offer here. A case built on delivery is: Alcon will very probably meet its EPS guidance.

Strongest counter-case. After the damage of 2025, management has every reason to set 2027 guidance low and rebuild a record of raising it. If the money reinvested in the fourth quarter of 2026 proves to be one-off, and Vivity Pro launches well, 2027 could be the first year of operating raises.

What would change my view. A 2027 EPS guide with a midpoint below about $3.75, set while management describes the business as on track, would tell me that management is building a cushion. A first-half raise earned in the business would matter more than any of the 2026 raises did.

Against the market. Mid-2026 broker notes described Alcon as a company that guides low and then raises. The full-year evidence does not support that description. I am more sceptical than the bulls about the raising record, and less worried than the bears about a cut to EPS guidance.

Conclusion: Alcon's guidance is realistic and well signalled but not conservative, its delivery record is good on EPS and poor on revenue, and its guidance raises have come from non-operating sources.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Sales or margin guidance was lowered or trimmed in each of 2024, 2025 (two cuts) and 2026, the 2026 raises were non-operating (buyback, tariff refund), revenue missed consensus in seven of nine quarters and the 2023 targets for 2027 are slipping, while EPS beats in seven of nine come from flexing costs and current guidance is realistic with no cushion. I sit below the group's 51 because the trims are consecutive and the mid-term targets will be missed, between Instalco's missed targets and Hexatronic's weak two-year record.

#5Pricing power, operating and financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Alcon's cost structure turns 5% revenue growth into about 10% EPS growth, but management reinvests about half of the operating leverage, which caps the upside and steadies the result.

Evidence: operating leverage. In normal years 38% to 45% of each extra dollar of revenue has reached core operating profit. In 2025 the figure was 2%, because currency, tariffs and acquired research absorbed the gain; on the way down in 2020 it was 79%. Because the cost base is largely fixed, one point of revenue growth is worth about 2% of operating profit, or $0.07 to $0.10 of EPS.

Evidence: what happens to that leverage. Management reinvests about half of it every year. It spent two-thirds of the 2026 tariff refund, and it holds research spending at the top of its 7% to 9% of sales range. The $80 million of savings landing in 2027 is earmarked to offset inflation and tariffs, so under half of the savings reaches the margin. The result is a net margin gain of 60 to 100bp a year.

Evidence: price. Price adds 1.0% to 1.5% to group revenue a year, almost all of it from United States contact lenses (two price increases in the first half of 2026) and eye drops, and wage and materials inflation consume nearly all of that gain. In premium cataract lenses Alcon's pricing is negative: Alcon holds list prices and defends share through rebates, while PureSee sells about 15% below Vivity in Europe.

Evidence: financial leverage and feedback loops. Alcon's gearing is too low to amplify earnings; the buyback adds about 1 point a year to EPS growth. The reinforcing feedback loops are slow and positive: installed consoles feed consumables sales, and new contact lens capacity feeds share and lowers unit cost. The one fast loop is negative: free samples of a rival's premium lens become a surgeon's habit.

Inference and so-what. Revenue growth of 5% does become EPS growth of about 10%, so Alcon passes the "outsized profit growth" test at a ratio of about two to one. That ratio, however, is capped by management's choice, not by the structure of the business. Management acts as a stabiliser of EPS in both directions: it cuts spending when revenue falls short and spends windfalls when they arrive. This behaviour makes Alcon's earnings more predictable and its positive surprises rarer at the same time. It is the single most useful thing to understand about how Alcon's results will read.

The swing factor for 2027 EPS
About $40 million of tariff-refund money was reinvested in the fourth quarter of 2026. Our base case assumes that 70% of this spending does not recur, and management has not said whether it will. Management's answer on 2 March 2027 is worth up to $0.07 of 2027 EPS between the two extremes.

Strongest counter-case. Management's cap on margin could lift: Pershing Square argues that the leverage is there to take margins above 25%, and the depressed share price gives management a reason to listen. Or the cap could tighten: if price stops covering inflation (no repeat of the 2026 contact lens increases), the annual margin gain shrinks by 30 to 40bp.

What would change my view. Two consecutive years in which more than half the gross leverage reaches the margin without one-off help. Alcon has never delivered more than 100bp of margin gain without such help in a year of 5% revenue growth or less.

Against the market. The FactSet median for 2028 implies a margin gain of 130bp, which assumes that management's cap lifts. On closer reading, the updated brokers do not assume that: their typical 2028 EPS growth is about 12.5%, the same as ours. The "stretched 2028 consensus" that our earlier research flagged is therefore about half the size it first appeared.

Conclusion: Alcon's business model converts 5% revenue growth into about 10% EPS growth, but management's habit of reinvesting half the leverage caps the upside and steadies the result, so pricing power and leverage protect Alcon's earnings more than they propel them.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. A largely fixed cost base gives 38-45% drop-through in normal years (79% on the way down in 2020), so a point of revenue is about 2% of operating profit, with slow positive installed-base loops and 200-300bp of identified cost scope; but price is absorbed by inflation (and negative in premium lenses), gearing is too low to amplify EPS, and management reinvests about half the leverage, so EPS grows about twice revenue, the ordinary ratio. Above the ordinary mix because the gross leverage and unused cost lever are structural, short of 75 because only one gear works and it is capped by choice; coherent with the groups' 55 and 53.

#6Forecast financials

The forecasts give EPS growth of about 10.5% a year to 2030 on about 5% revenue growth: the same pace as Alcon's past, with a new composition, and close to consensus.

The table's two EPS rows show one set of forecasts on two bases. The model applies our growth rates to FactSet's revenue figure, which is 0.8% above the company's, and divides by undiluted shares; together these choices lift the model's EPS about 2% above the like-for-like figure. Comparisons with the brokers should therefore use the second EPS row, on which we are about 1% below the updated brokers in each year from 2026 to 2028.

Is there double-digit growth, and is it better than the past? For EPS, yes: about 10.5% a year from 2026 to 2030. For revenue, no: about 5% a year, against 6.0% from 2022 to 2025. The core operating margin rises about 70bp a year, the same pace as from 2019 to 2024, and reaches around 2030 the level the company once promised for 2027. Alcon's growth is therefore the same as in the past, not higher. What is new is its composition. About one point a year now comes from a falling share count, where none did before 2026, and less growth comes from equipment and implants and more from consumables, contact lenses and eye-health products.

The 2027 forecast barely depends on a premium-lens recovery, but it depends more than the market realises on two drug launches. Of the 5.0 points of 2027 revenue growth, the three annuity lines supply about 3.6 points, the Tryptyr and ENCELTO launches about 1.1 points, and implants and equipment together only 0.3 points. The two drugs carry low margins, so a shortfall in their sales would cost revenue far more than EPS. Of the 9.5% EPS growth, about 5 points come from revenue, about 3 points from margin and about 1 point each from interest and the share count, less 0.8 points from a higher tax rate.

2027 is the trough year for EPS growth, and 2028 is the exposed year. The forecast 2028 margin gain of 100bp equals the best normal year on record. It assumes that the dilution from the Neurotech acquisition fades, while the model's cash-flow inputs assume $350 to $400 million of new acquisitions every year, each of which dilutes. I regard +100bp as the top of the plausible base.

Why I have changed no input. I lean in three directions, but none of the leanings is large enough to move an annual input. First, FY2026 EPS is as likely to land at $3.49 to $3.50 as at the model's $3.47, a difference of only 0.1 point of margin. Second, 2027 implant growth looks nearer 0% than the model's +1% once China's price cuts are dated to January, but the model sizes ENCELTO at about half of what management and three brokers expect, and the two effects offset. Third, the second-quarter 2027 margin will print nearer 21.0% than the model's 21.5%, because that quarter laps a $15 million licensee payment; the full year is unaffected.

Alcon generates more cash than the model's free cash flow line shows. The model's free cash flow ($1,478 million in 2027) is about $300 million a year below what the company's reported cash flow implies. The gap is not an error in the inputs. Share-based pay ($162 million in 2025) is a cost in core earnings but not a cash cost, and tax on the items excluded from core earnings is largely deferred. On the reported cash basis, net debt falls faster, to about 0.7x EBITDA by end-2028, which is why the choice between buybacks and acquisitions arrives soon.

Strongest counter-case. The forecasts could be too low if Alcon's premium-lens share recovers and operating leverage flows to the margin (EPS about 5% higher in 2027 and 7% higher in 2028), or too high if implant sales stay negative and the reinvestment recurs (EPS 5% and 7% lower).

What would change my view. The formal 2027 guide on 2 March and its margin bridge; United States implant growth in the May and August 2027 reports.

Against the market. In numbers, almost nothing separates our forecasts from the updated brokers'. Where I differ is on the quality of growth. The market widely sees 2026 EPS growth as flattered by about 4 points of one-offs. That is right, but Alcon's tax rate also rose from 17.4% to about 19.3%, which took 2 to 2.5 points off. Net of both effects, operating EPS grew 10% to 11% in a year when implant sales fell.

Conclusion: the forecasts give dependable EPS growth of about 10% to 11% a year on 5% revenue growth, the same as Alcon's past and not higher, with 2027 the trough year and the 2028 margin the most exposed assumption.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. About 10.5% sits just inside the 10-15% B band. I place it near the floor because the growth equals the past rather than beating it (revenue about 5% against 6.0% in 2022-25, margin up about 70bp a year as in 2019-24), about a point a year comes from the buyback, and the 2028 margin step is the top of the plausible range.

#7Scope for forecasts to lead to upgrades over 6 to 12 months

There is no gap between our numbers and consensus to exploit: guidance already says what we think, and the brokers are tightly bunched around it. Thirteen of the fourteen updated 2027 EPS estimates lie within $3.79 to $3.92. The brokers' 2027 revenue (growth of 5.8%) is 0.7% above ours, and Alcon usually misses on revenue.

Inside that revenue, two broker lines look wrong in opposite directions. The brokers' equipment line looks $60 to $70 million too high, given management's guidance that unit sales will be stable and a shift to a standalone console that sells for about half the price of the combined system. Their eye-health line looks about $80 million too low. The two errors cancel in the full year but not in the halves, because the equipment shortfall falls in the first half.

Two mechanical moves in consensus are coming that are not news. As old estimates are refreshed, the FactSet median for 2026 should rise about 1% and the median for 2028 should fall 1.5% to 2%. The 2028 move will register as downgrades.

Inference. Over the next 18 months, 2027 EPS consensus is twice as likely to be cut as raised. In substance, estimates are held; in appearance, they are cut slightly, and the appearance outlasts the substance by some months.

So-what. Upgrades to guidance and estimates are unlikely before the second half of 2027. The upgrade that is possible is to the narrative, and it needs United States implant growth to turn positive, which Alcon cannot report before August 2027.

Four developments would produce upgrades. None is in the base case, and the largest is the one management has not signalled.

The brokers let cash simply build on the balance sheet, and they carry little for the corneal cell therapy AURN001. A capital markets day that reset the mid-term targets and announced a cost programme and a larger buyback together would change 2028 to 2030 estimates in one day.

What would change my view. A formal 2027 guide set clearly below $3.80 would open room for raises through the year. A positive first-half implant figure in the United States would bring the narrative upgrade forward by a quarter.

Against the market. Bulls expect estimate upgrades from the new products in 2027. I think the new products mostly replace the contribution that equipment and implants no longer make. Bears expect a downgrade cycle. I think the cost line and the buyback prevent one.

Conclusion: the scope for guidance or estimate upgrades over the next 6 to 12 months is small, and the upgrade worth waiting for is to the narrative, no earlier than August 2027.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, has no cushion (the 2 March guide 55% within 1% of $3.84, 35% below, 10% above; a 2027 EPS cut at 25% slightly likelier than a raise at 20%), consensus is likelier cut (30%) than raised (15%) with the stale 2028 median due to fall 1.5-2%, and only the narrative offers an upgrade, not before August 2027. A small expected cut against 5% revenue growth puts it just below IMCD, consistent with the group's 44 and the level-25 description of no cushion and a stale consensus above updated brokers.

#8Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, share price, and peers

Alcon's momentum is negative on four of five counts; only the share price has improved, and that improvement belongs to the sector.

  • Guidance: trimmed in November after two raises earlier in 2026. The direction is sideways to down.
  • Estimates: FY2027 EPS consensus is down 1.1% over one month, 2.6% over three and 3.0% over twelve. Buy ratings are 65% of the total, down 12 points in six months. The dashboard rates sell-side earnings momentum F.
  • Narrative: "quality franchise, cheapest multiple, losing the premium lens battle, show me". No 2026 result was rewarded by the share price.
  • Share price: technical momentum is rated D, but the detail is more interesting than the letter. The shares are up 17% from CHF 52.42 on 13 October and stand 7% above their 200-day moving average, on rising volume. That average, however, has not risen in any of the last twelve months, and Alcon's relative strength is only at the 44th percentile.

Evidence: peers. In the sector, momentum goes to companies with a product cycle that earns price, such as Demant and Straumann. Companies without one, such as Smith & Nephew and Coloplast, sit at the floor. Within eye care, Cooper cut its growth guidance and fell 14% in a day, and Carl Zeiss Meditec is restructuring under a new chief executive. Johnson & Johnson's United States surgical vision business grew 14% in the third quarter, at Alcon's expense. All seven sector stocks rated F for earnings momentum, Alcon included, trade at or below the 5th percentile of their own multiple history.

Inference and so-what. The improvement in Alcon's share price is not one to lean on. Alcon's six-month return of +15.8% is identical to its peer basket's, so the rally was the sector's, and part of the sector's rally reflects money rotating into healthcare that can rotate out again. The market trades Alcon with the downgraded names (its closest co-movers are Smith & Nephew and Medacta), not with the product-cycle winners.

Strongest counter-case. A 17% rise through a disappointing quarter may mean the market is already looking past news it expected. Pershing Square bought during the de-rating, and bottoms form before the fundamentals turn.

What would change my view. The 200-day average turning up; the first result that the share price rewards; or estimates flat for three months, which would move Alcon out of the group pinned at the floor.

Against the market. Sell-side ratings are still mostly positive (65% buys, and a median target 18% above the share price), while estimates and the reaction to results are negative. That combination is not capitulation. I read the sell-side as more hopeful than the share price's behaviour since May justifies.

Conclusion: momentum in guidance, estimates and narrative is currently negative and the eye-care peers are weak, with only a sector-led share price recovery to set against them.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. Both measures below 50 give D, and the parts confirm it: guidance trimmed in November, FY2027 EPS down 1.1%/2.6%/3.0% over one, three and twelve months since Q3 (figures.md's +2.0% three-month reading predates the results), the Buy share down 12 points to 65%, no 2026 result rewarded and eye-care peers weak. The price is 17% off its October low and 7% above a flat 200-day average, but the rally matched the sector's, so I place it in the lower middle of the band.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and the case

The earnings case is simple and its risks are small; the share-price case is not simple, because it turns on one product line that only third parties measure, in a sector that sets the ceiling. The earnings rest on five product lines, three of them mechanical, and on a cost line managed to a number.

The five key judgements, with the arithmetic. All figures use the like-for-like base: FY2027 revenue $11,585 million, EPS $3.80, 482 million shares, tax at 20%; FY2028 revenue $12,199 million, EPS $4.27, 478 million shares.

Three conclusions stand out from the table.

  • Judgement 1, the premium-lens share, is small for EPS and large for the share price. Its 1.7% EPS effect sits beside a multiple that would otherwise move 13% to 16% up, or 16% down to the 14.5x trough.
  • Judgements 1 and 2 partly offset each other, because management cuts spending when revenue disappoints. Treated as independent, the company-specific drivers combine to about 3.5% of EPS either way; in practice the range is narrower.
  • A larger buyback is a weaker EPS lever than it looks. At 17 times earnings, Alcon's earnings yield barely exceeds the after-tax cost of its debt. The value of a larger buyback lies in its signal, and in being the alternative to a dilutive acquisition.

The range of likely EPS outcomes is narrow. With about 80% confidence, FY2027 EPS lands at $3.62 to $3.95, weighted slightly to the lower half, and FY2028 EPS at $4.00 to $4.50.

Sudden risks to the earnings are external and unlikely in any one year; sudden risks to the share price are frequent. The fundamental risks that could arrive suddenly are currency (unhedged in translation), tariffs, and a quality or supply event. The risk to the share price is frequent, sudden and partly unjustified by fundamentals: moves of 10% to 15% on implant headlines have precedent.

The margin half of the case is highly trackable, and soon (2 March 2027); the premium-lens half is not. Alcon does not disclose its United States premium share, third-party sources differ by 5 to 8 points (66% on one survey of busy clinics, mid-50s on one broker's national estimate), and China's price cuts will distort the reported implant line in the first half of 2027.

The test to watch
Watch United States implant growth together with third-party share data, not Alcon's reported implant growth. The best early indicator is a competitor's figure: Johnson & Johnson's United States surgical vision growth, published about three weeks before each Alcon report.

Two balance-sheet items to watch. Inventories rose $241 million in the first nine months of 2026, more than in all of 2025, while the product lines they serve slowed. And Unity consoles can be placed with no upfront payment, with revenue recognised at placement under finance leases. Neither item is a problem today, but both are where a second problem would show first.

Sector precedents. Medtech punishes slow growth twice, in earnings and in the multiple: Carl Zeiss Meditec fell from 37x to 16x over three years. Those disappointments came from single points of failure in earnings (China at Zeiss, one sales channel at Cooper, United States orthopaedics at Smith & Nephew). Alcon has no single point of failure in its earnings; its single point of failure is in its valuation. Alcon's own precedents are encouraging on duration: each premium-lens share swing since 2019 ran 12 to 24 months and ended with an Alcon launch.

Strongest counter-case. Bausch + Lomb plans a competing premium lens in the same class in 2027, which could restart free sampling to surgeons just as PureSee's sampling fades.

What would change my view. United States implant sales still falling in the August 2027 report, with Johnson & Johnson's surgical vision business still growing at double digits.

Against the market. The market prices all of Alcon's earnings as if they were at risk. In fact, a further five-point loss of United States premium share would cost under 2% of EPS.

Conclusion: fundamental risk is low, bounded and trackable, while share-price risk is concentrated in one hard-to-measure product line and in external shocks, so the case is simple in its earnings and less simple in its valuation.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. The earnings case is narrow and simple: a FY2027 EPS cone of $3.62-3.95 around $3.80 (about -5%/+4% at 80% confidence), three of five lines mechanical, 1.4x net debt 98% fixed-rate, low cyclicality and self-offsetting drivers. Held off 75 by unhedged currency (3.8% of EPS for a 3% dollar move), possible tariffs (-2% to -7%) and a share price that turns on an undisclosed US premium-lens share with 10-15% headline moves and a sector-set multiple, so just below MITIE and nearer the detailed risks group (68) than the first layer (57).

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Alcon is bottoming, not turning: the evidence for a bottom is solid, but the turn cannot be evidenced before August 2027. The dashboard's rule puts Alcon in the Bottoming phase, and I agree.

For bottoming: the multiple is at its floor; estimate cuts are shallow, not accelerating; the 2027 bad news has been pre-announced; the company and a new long-term holder (Pershing Square) are buying; and the share price has lifted off its October low.

Against turning up: estimates are still falling; the 200-day average is flat; no 2026 result was rewarded; the share of buy ratings is still sliding; and the next three reports lean negative.

Inference and so-what. This is a bottom with a long base, not a turn. The move to "turning up" has a dated path, in this order:

  1. Johnson & Johnson's United States surgical vision growth slows from 14% (reported mid-January and mid-April 2027).
  2. Estimates stop falling in substance (after the 2 March guide).
  3. United States implant growth turns positive (August 2027 at the earliest).
  4. A result is rewarded by the share price.

On sector precedent, a re-rating needs two consecutive positive implant quarters, which points to August to November 2027. After that, the comparisons ease for three reports in a row, which is when the investment case could broaden.

Waiting for evidence costs the earnings carry, a little under 1% a month. The risk in waiting is that the first signal arrives in a competitor's report, three weeks before Alcon's own.

Strongest counter-case. The stock could slip back to stalling: if Vivity Pro does not stop the share loss, Alcon remains a 10% compounder on 14x to 17x earnings, cheap, growing and unloved. Alternatively, the turn may already have begun in October, with the share price ahead of the evidence.

What would change my view. Any two of the four steps above arriving early would move me to "turning up". A formal 2027 guide below our base, with a cut to 2027 consensus of more than 2%, would move me back toward stalling.

Against the market. The sell-side, by its ratings, treats the stock as already turning. The share price since May treats it as stalling. I sit between the two: bottoming, with the turn datable but not yet evidenced.

Conclusion: Alcon is bottoming, and the earliest it can be shown to be turning up on its own evidence is August 2027.

Score: 47, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's Bottoming over the computed Stalling: the multiple is at its floor, cuts are shallow, 2027's bad news is pre-announced, the company and a new holder are buying and earnings keep compounding at about 10%. But estimates are still falling, the 200-day average is flat, the Buy share is sliding, the next three reports lean negative and the turn cannot be evidenced before August 2027, so it sits just above Linea Directa's unforecast improvement and below Solid State's bottoming-to-turning.

#11The fair multiple

The 22.51x guideline multiple is a fair destination over three years but too high for 18 months: Alcon can earn about 19.5x to 20x by itself by March 2028, and the rest needs the sector. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a stock in the Bottoming phase is 22.51 times two-year-forward earnings, the 30th percentile of Alcon's own history. Today's multiple is 17.2x, so the guideline is 31% higher.

Four separate routes point to about 19.5x to 20x, or just below, as the multiple Alcon can earn by itself by March 2028.

  • Alcon's premium to its sector. The premium has averaged about 14% since the spin-off. Applied to today's sector median of 17.1x, it gives about 19.5x.
  • What upgraded peers command. The large-cap sector names with stable or rising estimates trade at 18.4x to 21.5x. None is above 21.5x.
  • What the bulls' own targets imply. The median broker target of $86 is about 20x today's two-year-forward EPS, and about 18x the equivalent EPS twelve months from now, when the target falls due. Brokers quote 21x to 25x, but on nearer-year earnings.
  • What the growth supports. A 10% to 11% compounder with a modest reinvestment runway merits 19x to 22x, as our first set of research concluded.

The remaining 12% to 15% to reach 22.51x needs the sector median multiple to rise from about 17x to nearly 20x. That rise depends on the discount rate and on flows between sectors; it is undated and outside Alcon's control. Reaching the guideline therefore needs two things to happen, Alcon controls only one of them, and the earliest that Alcon's part can be evidenced (August 2027) is seven months before the model's March 2028 horizon.

In favour of the guideline

22.51x is below Alcon's ten-year median of 24.2x and matches its five-year median of 22.6x. The guideline sets a low multiple for the Bottoming phase because forecasts are usually uncertain in that phase, but Alcon's forecasts are unusually certain; what is uncertain is the narrative. Quality franchises at floor multiples do revert.

Against the guideline

Alcon's history includes 2019 to 2021, when near-zero interest rates put the shares on 25x to 30x and growth was faster than the 5% on offer now. The gap between core and reported earnings also argues for some discount to cleaner compounders.

The downside multiple is 14.5x, just below the five-year low of 14.95x and equivalent to the share price of five weeks ago.

What would change my view. A sector median back above 19x would make the guideline reachable within 18 months. Implant sales growing 3% or more, with estimates rising, would justify the top of the peer range, 21.5x, without the sector's help.

Against the market. The buy-rated brokers' targets imply 18x to 20x, at or just below my range. Pershing Square's implied view is higher. The share price says 17x is right until proven otherwise.

Conclusion: I regard 22.51x as reasonable over three years, but it is 12% to 15% above the 19.5x to 20x that Alcon can earn alone by March 2028.

Score: 82, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and neutral on the other gives B. Part of the cheapness is deserved (the history includes 25-30x in the zero-rate, faster-growth 2019-21 years, core flatters reported earnings, the premium-lens moat has narrowed), but a Bottoming business with unusually certain earnings and a peer reading near the cheap threshold warrants the upper half of the band.

#12Total shareholder return

The return is a dependable earnings leg of about 10% to 11% a year plus an undated re-rating; on my weights that gives about +20% to +25% to March 2028, under half the model's +52.9%.

The return at the guideline multiple, from the model.

To 30 September 2029+73.1%+21.0%CHF 106.21+31.0%+30.8%+1.6%

The earnings and multiple parts multiply; the dividend part adds. Returns are in francs at a constant exchange rate.

  • Earnings (+16.1%, then +31.0%): the reliable part. This part is two-year-forward EPS rolling forward at about 11% a year, built each year from about 5 points of revenue growth, 3 to 5 points of margin, 1 point of interest and 1 point of share count. It needs no lens recovery and nothing Alcon has not done before.
  • The multiple (+30.8%): the unreliable part. This part is a single step from 17.2x to 22.51x, taken in full by March 2028. Because the step is the same in both horizons, the annualised return falls from 36% to 21%.
  • Dividends (about 0.5% a year): small by design. The payout is about 10% of core earnings, and cash returns come mainly through the buyback, which shows up in the earnings part.

The return at other multiples.

Guideline 22.51x+52.9%+73.1%10% to 15%

Inference and so-what. Weighted, the return to March 2028 is about +20% to +25%, a little under half the model's figure. Over three years, on weights shifted modestly toward a re-rating (15%, 25%, 40% and 20% down the table), the return is about +45%, or 14% a year. Two features of the return matter more than the precise weights.

First, the return is asymmetric in time. The earnings leg compounds whatever the multiple does, so the trough case loses about 6% over 16 months, whereas the same trough multiple applied today would lose 16% before any cut to estimates. Over three years the trough case roughly breaks even, so the case is stronger over three years than over 18 months.

Second, with no re-rating the return equals the earnings growth rate, about 10% to 11% a year. That is the return the case earns if the premium-lens worry neither clears nor worsens.

Currency. Alcon's earnings are in dollars and its main listing is in francs. A dollar that weakens against all currencies raises Alcon's dollar EPS by about 1.25% for each 1% fall, which roughly offsets the translation loss for a franc-based holder. A rise in the franc alone has no such offset, because Alcon's franc costs exceed its franc revenues.

Strongest counter-case. The guideline could be reached on time: if the sector re-rates in 2027 and Vivity Pro works, 22.5x is no more than Alcon's five-year median. Or my floor could be too high: a sector capitulation together with a failed launch would test 13x on lower estimates, about 30% below today's price if it happened at once.

What would change my view. The four steps in topic #10 would raise the weight on the upper two rows of the table. A large acquisition, or United States implant sales still falling in August 2027, would raise the weight on the lower two.

Against the market. The median broker target implies about +18% over twelve months, between my unchanged-multiple row and my 19.5x to 20x row. The model's return is well above both.

Conclusion: the return is a dependable earnings leg of about 10% to 11% a year plus an undated re-rating, which gives about +20% to +25% to March 2028 on my weights, against the model's +52.9% at the guideline multiple, and a better balance over three years than over 18 months.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. About +23% sits in the 20-35% B band at about 78 on the scale, with a supportive three-year check and a thin lower tail (the trough multiple on estimates 5-7% lower loses only about 6%, because the earnings leg compounds through it). I take a point off because about half the central return rests on a re-rating that needs the lens worry to clear and the sector to recover, neither in Alcon's control.

#13Summary conclusion

Alcon is a strong franchise with one exposed edge, valued as if the edge were the whole company. Its earnings need nothing unproven and should compound at about 10% a year. They are also unlikely to surprise upward, because management spends the upside and guidance holds no cushion. This is therefore a case about valuation and time, not about upgrades.

For Richard's decisionThe positive skew is present in the multiple and absent in the estimates. The multiple is at its floor, the earnings carry the holder through the trough case with little loss, and the trigger for a re-rating has a date. But the next six months are more likely to confirm known negatives than to resolve them, the trigger cannot be evidenced before August 2027, and the full guideline multiple needs the sector's help.

The practical questions are therefore about sequence. Each question has a date, and each answer moves the weights in topic #12:

  1. Mid-January and mid-April 2027: does Johnson & Johnson's United States surgical vision growth slow from 14%?
  2. 2 March 2027: what does Alcon's management say about its fourth-quarter spending, a cost programme and its balance sheet?
  3. August 2027: is Alcon's United States implant growth positive?

The four memo ratings:

  • Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: C. The forces under way sustain about 10% EPS growth, but none raises the trajectory, and the one that could re-rate the shares, Vivity Pro, is unproven until mid-2027.
  • Foundations' Robustness: B. Number-one positions in tight oligopolies, a 70% annuity and low gearing, held back from an A by a narrowing premium-lens moat, the gap between core and reported earnings, and weak returns on acquisitions.
  • Setups' Fit/Crispness: C. The case fits "cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a first-quartile multiple" in every respect except that the concern is not yet clearing, and the reversion to a normal multiple also needs the sector.
  • Case Riskiness: B. Earnings are predictable to within about 5% and the trough case loses little over time, but the share price hangs on one hard-to-measure product line and on unhedged currency and tariffs.

The Rater on the four memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 53, set by the Rater. The input forces roughly offset, a slightly negative external balance (topic 1, 46) against gently positive internal change that does not raise the trajectory (topic 2, 56), and the output is about 10.5% EPS growth (topic 6), the Universe median and the same as Alcon's past. So the change reaches profits surely but is not material: a mild net positive, as the memo's C implies.

Foundations' Robustness: 79, set by the Rater. Quality (topic 3, 71) rests on number-one positions in tight, barrier-protected oligopolies, a 70% lock-in annuity, non-cyclical demand, low fixed-rate gearing and EPS predictable within about 5%, and in Richard's CVS terms that stability outweighs a reported return on capital that is not high. The delivery record (topic 4, 42), the narrowing premium-lens moat and the core-to-reported gap are the ordinary parts that hold it just below Hellenic Telecom and Avanza, in line with the memo's B.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 72, set by the Rater. The case fits 'cause for concern clearing in a high-quality, low-cyclicality business on a first-quartile multiple' in substance, with the quality, low cyclicality, floor multiple and a narrow concern (premium lenses, about 4-5% of sales) all present. The clearing element is loose because today's problems (US implants negative, a third rival lens and China cuts in 2027) have not begun to clear, which in Richard's Judges Scientific terms holds it just below 75; the sector re-rating it needs is timing and price, judged in topics 7 and 12, so not counted here.

Case Riskiness: 74, set by the Rater. Over topic 9 (70), the earnings case is boring and its risks are mostly paper cuts (a 5% EPS cone, low fixed-rate gearing, a trough case losing about 6% over 16 months) with the multiple at the bottom of its range, which in Richard's CVS terms reduces the risk of a large fall. It stays below CVS's 80-85 because guidance is realistic rather than conservative, currency is unhedged, tariffs could take up to 7% of EPS and the share price swings 10-15% on an undisclosed lens share.

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

  • FY2025 earnings per share: 3.07 on the brokers' basis against 1.88 on our model's basis (+63.2%).

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Hybrid bond coupons and capitalised leases are not in the data file; check the company's reporting where relevant.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
